section_summary: This section (pages 1–64) consists of U.S. State Department diplomatic despatches, consular telegrams, internal Far Eastern Affairs memoranda, and translated foreign press reports from January and February 1939 regarding political affairs in Japan. Primary focus is given to the fall of Prince Fumimaro Konoe's Cabinet and the installation of Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma's Cabinet, analyzing internal friction caused by Home Minister Admiral Nobumasa Suetsugu's totalitarian drive, business opposition to wartime economic controls, and implications for relations with the Soviet Union and Western powers. The documents also examine Prime Minister Hiranuma's and Foreign Minister Hachiro Arita's addresses to the 74th Diet, Diet interpellations on the Open Door and potential Western sanctions, Soviet commentary from Izvestiya and Krasnaya Zvezda, and the further implementation of the National General Mobilization Law.

subfiles.about: A concluding roster listing Japanese higher civil service investigators, administrative secretaries, and a counselor.
subfiles.summary: Roster continuation lists nine investigators and six administrative secretaries in Japan's higher civil service, including Shiozawa, Shiraichi, Adachi, Tenbo, and Itagaki, continuing a personnel enclosure.
subfiles.title: Roster of Japanese Higher Civil Service Officials [Continuation]

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting that the text of the Japanese Foreign Minister's annual address was cabled to the United States for distribution via Domei News Agency.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Foreign Minister Arita's annual address text was telegraphed to the U.S., distributed via Domei News Agency, filed at 894.00/837.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 40 on Distribution of Foreign Minister Arita's Address

subfiles.about: State Department Document File Note referencing decimal file 894.00/838.
subfiles.summary: Standard document file note bears only decimal number 894.00/838, with no substantive text.
subfiles.title: Document File Note Regarding Decimal File 894.00/838

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting on Diet interpellations concerning Japanese foreign policy, the Open Door in China, and potential Western economic sanctions.
subfiles.summary: Grew reviews Diet interpellations criticizing Arita's Open-Door accommodation with Britain/U.S. as abandoning the China-Manchukuo economic bloc; Arita promised respecting third-party rights, while Hiranuma said Japan was prepared for economic sanctions or blockades.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 44 on Diet Interpellations Regarding Foreign Policy and the Open Door

subfiles.about: Telegram summarizing Shanghai press and puppet regime reactions to Foreign Minister Arita's Diet address.
subfiles.summary: Gauss relays Shanghai press reactions to Arita's Diet speech: Anglo-American papers dismissed it as confirming a closing Open Door, Chinese papers were skeptical, while pro-Japanese outlets welcomed the East Asian New Order and a unified Chinese government.
subfiles.title: Shanghai Telegram No. 69 on Local Press Reaction to Foreign Minister Arita's Speech

subfiles.about: Telegram detailing Foreign Minister Arita's statements in the Lower House Budget Committee on economic cooperation, indemnities, extraterritoriality, and recognition of a new Chinese government.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Arita telling the Budget Committee Japan sought an economic bloc with China/Manchukuo without excluding third parties, no war indemnity, possible relinquishing extraterritoriality and concessions, and expecting regional Chinese regimes to soon unify for recognition.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 47 on Foreign Minister Arita's Budget Committee Statements

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing Soviet press analyses of the Japanese Cabinet change transmitted from Moscow.
subfiles.summary: Salisbury summarizes Moscow Despatch 2020: Soviet commentary blamed Konoe's fall on military-financial rifts and Western credits to China, seeing Hiranuma's rise as more China aggression, fascisization, and anti-war suppression.
subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Moscow Despatch No. 2020

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting translations and Russian clippings of articles from Izvestiya and Krasnaya Zvezda analyzing the downfall of the Konoe Cabinet and formation of the Hiranuma Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires ad interim Alexander C. Kirk transmits translations and original Russian press clippings of articles published on January 9, 1939, in Izvestiya (by V. Yuriev) and Krasnaya Zvezda (by M. Volkov). Both commentaries attribute the fall of Prince Konoe's Cabinet to the ruinous financial drain of the China war, fierce resistance by financial magnates against dividend restrictions under the National General Mobilization Law, and diplomatic setbacks following American and British loans to China. Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma is depicted as an ultra-reactionary leader of the fascist Kokuhonsha whose cabinet represents a compromise between the military and court/financial circles to continue the war in China and intensify the exploitation of Japanese workers. The Soviet authors conclude that Hiranuma will be unable to overcome Japan's mounting internal and external contradictions.
subfiles.title: Moscow Despatch No. 2020: Soviet Press Comment on Change of Cabinet in Japan

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Tokyo Telegram No. 41 concerning comments by a friend of Foreign Minister Arita regarding the Hiranuma Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Tokyo telegram reports an Arita friend saying Hiranuma's Cabinet misunderstood the world situation amid dominant military cliques.
subfiles.title: Document File Note Regarding Tokyo Telegram No. 41 (File 793.94/14642)

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 3600 on the Japanese Cabinet change and the enhanced possibility of war with Russia.
subfiles.summary: Salisbury summarizes Despatch 3600: Suetsugu's totalitarian schemes caused Konoe's resignation; reviews Embassy arguments for likelier 1939 Russo-Japanese conflict, questioning the claim reduced Chinese pressure favors Japan given risks of troop withdrawal.
subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 3600

subfiles.about: Despatch analyzing the resignation of the Konoe Cabinet, the composition of the Hiranuma Cabinet, and the heightened danger of an armed conflict between Japan and the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew provides an exhaustive review of the installation of the Hiranuma Cabinet following the resignation of Prince Fumimaro Konoe on January 4, 1939. Grew explains that the resignation was precipitated by acute cabinet discord caused by Home Minister Admiral Nobumasa Suetsugu's aggressive pushing of extreme measures—including press control, enhanced police powers, and a totalitarian single-party system—along with Konoe's weariness and lack of forceful leadership. The despatch provides an extensive biographical sketch of Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma, detailing his legal career, leadership of the ultra-nationalist Kokuhonsha, and service in the Privy Council. Grew concludes that while domestic policy will maintain continuity with Konoe's program, the danger of a Russo-Japanese war in 1939 has been significantly enhanced by Hiranuma's ideological background, the international fallout of the Munich Agreement, and persistent border and fishery frictions.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 3600: Japanese Cabinet Change, January 4-5, 1939

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum reviewing Tokyo Despatch No. 3638 and the opening addresses of Prime Minister Hiranuma and Foreign Minister Arita to the 74th Diet.
subfiles.summary: Ballantine summarizes Despatch 3638 on the 74th Diet: Hiranuma's vague speech foreshadowed more mobilization-law measures, coolly received; Arita affirmed continental policy, blamed status-quo powers for unrest, and reviewed third-power, Comintern, Chiang, and Soviet-fishery relations.
subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 3638

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting the opening addresses of Prime Minister Hiranuma and Foreign Minister Arita to the 74th Diet, with Japanese press commentary and full English texts.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits full English texts from The Japan Times of the annual Diet addresses delivered on January 21, 1939, by Prime Minister Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma and Foreign Minister Hachiro Arita. Grew observes that leading Japanese newspapers (Nichi Nichi, Yomiuri, Asahi, and Chugai Shogyo) expressed disappointment at Hiranuma's lack of concrete domestic policies, while strongly endorsing Arita's condemnation of status quo powers and urging closer alignment with Anti-Comintern partners. Attached clippings include Hiranuma's speech calling for national spiritual unity, service to the Throne, and permanent economic controls, and Arita's speech citing Manchukuo's development as proof of Japan's intentions while defending the New Order in East Asia against Western objections.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 3638: The Addresses of the Prime Minister and the Minister for Foreign Affairs at the Opening of the 74th Diet

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 3640 on vocational registration and the Cabinet Planning Board under the National General Mobilization Law.
subfiles.summary: Jones summarizes Despatch 3640: an Imperial Ordinance mandates registering five million skilled workers across 134 trades by March 1939, reorganizes the Planning Board under Aoki, drops dividend caps after business pushback, and questions regimentation's fit with Japanese character.
subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 3640

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting an English translation of an Imperial Ordinance establishing compulsory vocational registration under the National General Mobilization Law.
subfiles.summary: Grew transmits a translated Imperial Ordinance under the Mobilization Law establishing vocational registration for Japanese subjects, referencing earlier wartime-mobilization reporting.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 3640: Further Implementation of the National General Mobilization Law [Cover Page]
